CONTENT CARD:
The writer is encountering a chicken-and-egg dilemma. A person may be so far inside their child-state they cannot become the needed adult. Providing love is easier if one can already access at least one of their adult roles. Without that, the person might try speaking loving words while the inherited critic, numbness, panic, or urge to escape dominates the process.

ATTENTION AND CAUSAL PLAN:
- Situation: deep in child-state; needing an adult response while unable to access it.
- Contradiction: providing love is easier with at least one adult role already available—the very access that may be missing.
- Attempt under strain: loving words spoken while inherited critic, numbness, panic, or urge to escape dominates.
- Causal turn: difficulty accessing the needed adult leaves the attempt uncertain.

Facts to preserve: chicken-and-egg dilemma; “may,” not inevitability; at least one adult role. No proper names or attribution supplied.

Return publication prose only.

CONTENT CARD:
The body's trauma reactions may persist after objective danger is over, even when the person knows consciously that they are safe. With complex/developmental trauma, directly working on the deepest memory can overwhelm someone; gentle gradual work around the edges may suffice. Attribution: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron uses the phrase 'feather touch' for gentle approach; Peter Levine, founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle edge-work 'pendulation'. There is a parallel in inner-child therapy: knowing what the younger part needs is not enough when one is so absorbed in the child-state that adult perspective is insufficient to offer it.

ATTENTION AND CAUSAL PLAN:
- Danger has ended; the person knows they are safe; the body’s trauma reactions persist.
- Felt contradiction: conscious knowledge of safety does not necessarily shift the bodily state.
- With complex/developmental trauma, approaching the deepest memory directly can overwhelm → gentle, gradual work around the edges may suffice.
- Inner-child parallel: knowing the younger part’s needs does not ensure access to enough adult perspective to meet them while absorbed in the child-state.

Facts to preserve: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron → “feather touch”; Peter Levine, founder of Somatic Experiencing → “pendulation.” Preserve “may persist,” “can overwhelm,” and “may suffice”; the inner-child connection is a parallel.

ORIGINAL SOURCE SENTENCES (for exact fidelity checking; do not adopt their rhythm or sequence unless those are genuinely needed):
Physical trauma reactions can persist after the danger has passed, even when you know you're safe. With complex or developmental trauma, direct work on the deepest memory can be overwhelming, so a gradual approach may be enough: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron calls it a “feather touch,” and Peter Levine, the founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle work around the edges “pendulation.” The same limit appears in inner-child therapy: you can know what the younger part needs yet enter the child-state so fully that too little adult perspective remains to provide it.
